title: Projection-based segregated, iterative, and multi-stage physics-informed neural network for incompressible Navier-stokes equations
authors: Zhenyu Zhang, Zhixiang Ling, Yinghao Huo, Huayong Liu, Yunde Su
abstract: Physics-informed neural networks(PINNs) offer a mesh-free and continuously differentiable approach to fluid simulation. However, standard monolithic PINNs for incompressible Navier-Stokes (NS) equations often suffer from severe constraint coupling and spectral biases, limiting both convergence and accuracy. To address this challenge, we propose a segregated, iterative, and multi-stage PINN (SIM-PINN) inspired by the classical projection method in computational fluid dynamics. In SIM-PINN, the nonlinear NS equations are decoupled into the linearized momentum and pressure Poisson equations. Each is addressed separately using dedicated multi-stage neural networks and coupled through projection-based inner iterations. Each stage of the multi-stage neural networks for the momentum equations corresponds to one iteration of the projection method, in which the velocity fields are progressively refined at targeted frequencies. Upon iteration convergence, solutions to the fully coupled and nonlinear NS equations are recovered. By integrating the segregated and iterative framework with the multi-stage training, SIM-PINN alleviates the optimization difficulties of the incompressible NS equations arising from nonlinearity, constraint coupling, and spectral biases. The improved convergence and accuracy are demonstrated by simulations of steady lid-driven cavity and unsteady Kolmogorov flows.

infographic.key_insight: SIM-PINN combines projection-based segregation, iteration, and multi-stage training to reduce constraint coupling and spectral bias in incompressible flow simulation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach offers a mesh-free route to more accurate and better-converged incompressible Navier–Stokes solutions.
method: Decouple Navier–Stokes into linearized momentum and pressure Poisson equations solved by dedicated neural networks.
Couple velocity and pressure through projection-based inner iterations.
Use successive momentum-network stages to refine velocity at targeted frequencies.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports improved convergence and accuracy on steady lid-driven cavity and unsteady Kolmogorov flows, without numerical performance metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Computational cost and scalability remain unclear because the abstract does not quantify the overhead of iterative, multi-network training.
infographic.paper_title: Projection-based segregated, iterative, and multi-stage physics-informed neural network for incompressible Navier-stokes equations

title: Extensions to the Navier-Stokes-Fourier Equations for Rarefied Transport: Entropy Variable Formulation, Heat Transfer and Dispersion of a Non-Linear Entropy Stable Closure
authors: Frimpong A. Baidoo, Narayana R. Aluru, Thomas J. R. Hughes, Michael R. A. Abdelmalik
abstract: We assess the non-linear version of the Entropy Stable Extension to the Navier-Stokes-Fourier equations which were originally derived in arXiv:2407.17334. Using an identity for the derivative of the inverse of linearized collision operator, we show that the Entropy Stable Extension takes the form of a fourth-order quasi-cubic system of equations when written in entropy variables. Furthermore, we find that the quasi-linear contributions to the extension retain the highest order derivative contributions and the entropy stability of the full extension. This quasi-linear approximation is applied to the stationary heat transfer between parallel plates where we find that a specification of the boundary conditions that interpolates between the continuum and collisions limits can yield temperature profiles that better agree with DSMC predictions than Navier-Stokes-Fourier equations with Smoluchowski boundary conditions, while also giving a heat flux prediction that better agrees with the Sherman-Lees heat flux than the Navier-Stokes-Fourier prediction. We conclude with a brief study of dispersion of plane waves according to the linearized equations in one dimension where we show that all frequency modes are stable and relate this to entropy stability.

infographic.key_insight: The nonlinear entropy-stable extension of Navier–Stokes–Fourier forms a fourth-order quasi-cubic system in entropy variables, while a quasi-linear approximation preserves its highest-order terms and entropy stability.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The closure offers a promising continuum-model route to improved rarefied-gas heat-transfer predictions beyond standard Navier–Stokes–Fourier equations.
method: Reformulate the extension in entropy variables using an inverse collision-operator derivative identity.
Apply the quasi-linear approximation to stationary heat transfer between parallel plates.
Analyze plane-wave dispersion for the one-dimensional linearized equations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Parallel-plate temperature profiles agree better with DSMC and heat flux agrees better with Sherman–Lees than the stated Navier–Stokes–Fourier comparisons; all modes in the linearized dispersion analysis are stable.
infographic.watch_item: The heat-transfer improvement relies on boundary conditions interpolating between continuum and collisionless limits, and the reported tests do not establish performance in complex multidimensional flows.
infographic.paper_title: Extensions to the Navier-Stokes-Fourier Equations for Rarefied Transport: Entropy Variable Formulation, Heat Transfer and Dispersion of a Non-Linear Entropy Stable Closure

title: Boundary Layers, Displacement Flow, and the High-Frequency Response of Porous Media: Beyond the Viscous and Thermal Characteristic Lengths, Order by Order
authors: D. Lafarge, A. Bouchendouka, Z. E. A. Fellah
abstract: The Johnson-Koplik-Dashen viscous characteristic length $Λ$ and its thermal analogue $Λ'$ introduced by Champoux and Allard govern the leading $O(ω^{-1/2})$ boundary-layer behaviour of fluid-saturated porous media, but omit higher microgeometric effects associated with interface curvature and field gradients. We develop the asymptotic high-frequency expansions of dynamic tortuosity and dynamic compressibility beyond the leading boundary-layer terms. By resolving the oscillatory Stokes and heat conduction problems in the thin boundary-layer limit, we establish a recursive hierarchy, which can be continued to any order, defining successive microgeometric parameters, given by wall integrals. Each order requires transport equations of WKB type across the boundary layer, closed by a non-secularity condition, together with one Neumann problem for the potential displacement flow that the boundary layer induces. Applied to the values fitted on highly absorbing foams, these expressions show that the negative surface parameter is consistent with strong in-parallel disorder of the pore sizes, whereas the large positive third-order term points to strong constrictions or enlargements along part of the flow paths. The thermal parameters reduce to geometrical quantities: the integral mean curvature of the pore walls, a Willmore-type measure of their departure from umbilicity and, at the next order, this measure weighted by the mean curvature. Using the Avellaneda-Torquato relaxation-mode representation, we show that all these parameters are spectral data of the distribution of relaxation times. For isolated sharp edges across which the fluid flows, the singular terms of the formal expansion cancel, and the description persists with apparent, logarithmically varying values of the parameters.

infographic.key_insight: A recursive high-frequency expansion extends porous-media response beyond viscous and thermal characteristic lengths, capturing higher-order effects of pore-wall geometry and induced displacement flow.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These corrections can improve interpretation of acoustic response in porous absorbers by linking fitted parameters to pore-size disorder, constrictions, and enlargements.
method: Resolve oscillatory Stokes flow and heat conduction in thin boundary layers.
Compute successive wall-integral parameters using WKB-type transport equations and a Neumann problem for induced displacement flow.
Relate higher-order parameters to relaxation-time spectra through the Avellaneda–Torquato representation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Application to parameters fitted for highly absorbing foams supports geometric interpretations of negative surface and large positive third-order terms; the abstract reports no quantitative validation metrics.
infographic.watch_item: The expansion is asymptotic at high frequency, and sharp edges introduce apparent parameters that vary logarithmically rather than remaining constant.
infographic.paper_title: Boundary Layers, Displacement Flow, and the High-Frequency Response of Porous Media: Beyond the Viscous and Thermal Characteristic Lengths, Order by Order

title: CFD-driven symbolic regression of RANS transition models
authors: Louenas Zemmour, Xavier Gloerfelt, Paola Cinnella
abstract: Laminar-turbulent transition governs skin friction, heat transfer and losses in turbomachinery, yet Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) transition models rely on empirical correlations and hand-calibrated activation functions whose structural deficiencies cannot be resolved by recalibration. We propose a CFD-driven sparse symbolic regression framework to learn interpretable, closed-form corrections to the production and destruction activation functions in the intermittency equation of the local, Galilean-invariant $k$-$ω$-$γ$ model of Ge et al. Each correction combines a polynomial of a local pressure-gradient parameter, controlling amplitude and sign, with a bounded exponential of local flow features, controlling spatial support. This construction bounds the corrections without ad hoc limiters. Coefficients are identified by gradient-free optimization with the RANS solver in the loop, accelerated by POD-Kriging field surrogates, using mean-velocity data from wall-resolved large-eddy simulations (LES) of the ERCOFTAC T3 flat-plate cases. Elastic-net hyperparameters are selected automatically through bi-level optimization with leave-one-case-out cross-validation. The resulting model retains 11 of 21 candidate terms, compared with 20 under conventional grid-search tuning, while achieving comparable or slightly better accuracy on training and unseen cases. Both approaches recover the same leading-order correction. Applied without retraining to the transonic LS89 turbine cascade, far beyond the training envelope, the augmented model remains numerically robust and improves heat-transfer predictions at all four operating points, reducing errors by up to 70% where the baseline predicts premature transition under high freestream turbulence. Residual errors in transition onset and length highlight the limits of training on flat-plate data alone.

infographic.key_insight: CFD-driven symbolic regression learns compact, interpretable RANS transition-model corrections that improve predictions beyond the flat-plate training cases.
infographic.engineering_relevance: More accurate transition modeling can improve turbomachinery heat-transfer and loss predictions without abandoning practical RANS simulations.
method: Correct production and destruction activation functions in the local k–ω–γ intermittency model using bounded symbolic expressions.
Fit coefficients with gradient-free, solver-in-the-loop optimization accelerated by POD–Kriging field surrogates.
Select elastic-net hyperparameters through bi-level optimization and leave-one-case-out cross-validation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Trained on ERCOFTAC T3 flat-plate LES velocity data, the model retained 11 of 21 candidate terms and, without retraining, improved LS89 turbine-cascade heat-transfer predictions at all four operating points, reducing errors by up to 70%.
infographic.watch_item: Residual transition-onset and transition-length errors show that flat-plate training alone does not fully capture turbine-cascade transition physics.
infographic.paper_title: CFD-driven symbolic regression of RANS transition models

title: On the aerodynamics of an accelerating and decelerating propeller in hover at low Reynolds numbers
authors: Manuel Ratz, Christophe Schram, A. Sciacchitano, Miguel A. Mendez
abstract: Small unmanned aerial vehicles commonly regulate propeller thrust through rapid changes in rotational speed, yet it remains unclear how the inflow, the wake, and the near-surface velocity respond to these changes at low Reynolds numbers. A commercial two-bladed propeller was tested in hover with custom blade holders at three additional pitch offsets relative to the original blade geometry, $Θ=\,$0, 5, and $10^\circ$, and accelerated and decelerated between 3000 and 5000 RPM with open-loop step responses. The resulting nondimensional acceleration and deceleration numbers, below 0.011 and 0.007, suggest negligible acceleration effects. Phase-locked particle image velocimetry (PIV) at 40, 60, and $80\,\%$ rotor radius and in the meridian plane was combined with load measurements. The thrust coefficient responds quasi-steadily at $Θ= 10^\circ$, but shows hysteresis at the higher pitch offsets, with lower values during acceleration and higher values during deceleration than under steady conditions. This trend opposes expectations from dynamic inflow theory. The effect is largest at $Θ= 5^\circ$, with deviations from the steady values of up to 8\,% during acceleration and $5\,\%$ during deceleration, compared with $4\,\%$ and $3\,\%$ at $Θ= 10^\circ$. PIV reveals that the rotor-disk inflow, blade deformation, and sectional circulation remain largely quasi-steady, whereas velocity fluctuations, blade-wake vorticity, and tip-vortex circulation vary strongly, with the largest deviations at low rotational speeds rather than at peak acceleration or deceleration.

infographic.key_insight: Low-Reynolds-number propeller speed changes can produce thrust hysteresis even when rotor-disk inflow, blade deformation, and sectional circulation remain largely quasi-steady.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Steady thrust maps may misestimate transient thrust during rapid speed commands in small UAVs, with implications for control accuracy.
method: Tested a two-bladed propeller in hover at pitch offsets of 0°, 5°, and 10°.
Applied open-loop acceleration and deceleration steps between 3000 and 5000 RPM.
Combined load measurements with phase-locked PIV at 40%, 60%, and 80% rotor radius and in the meridian plane.
infographic.evidence_signal: At the 5° pitch offset, thrust-coefficient deviations reached 8% during acceleration and 5% during deceleration; flow-field departures were greatest at low rotational speeds rather than peak acceleration.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract inconsistently describes the 10° case as both quasi-steady and exhibiting deviations; verify pitch-dependent conclusions in the full paper before implementation.
infographic.paper_title: On the aerodynamics of an accelerating and decelerating propeller in hover at low Reynolds numbers

title: Bayesian Kolmogorov-Arnold networks for trustworthy Reynolds-stress closures
authors: Ali Eidi, Kherlen Jigjid, Tyler Buchanan, Richard P. Dwight
abstract: Data-driven turbulence closures can improve Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) predictions, but their use is limited by two issues: learned constitutive relations are often difficult to inspect, and predictions typically lack reliable uncertainty estimates. We develop a Bayesian tensor-basis Kolmogorov-Arnold network (BKAN) for Reynolds-stress anisotropy that addresses both within a single closure. Learnable univariate spline functions on network edges provide an inspectable representation that can, where sufficiently simple, be approximated symbolically. Variational posteriors over spline coefficients yield a predictive distribution separating epistemic uncertainty, due to limited training data, from aleatoric uncertainty, the irreducible scatter of high-fidelity targets at given inputs. Galilean and rotational invariance, symmetry, and tracelessness are enforced through the tensor basis, while physical realisability is treated separately through soft regularisation. A controlled regression benchmark assesses predictive accuracy, calibration, and Bayesian parameterisation. Placing the posterior on spline coefficients gives the best overall balance of accuracy, calibration, parameter cost, and interpretability. Applied to Reynolds-stress anisotropy, the BKAN is accurate in distribution, with calibrated, informative uncertainty that tends to identify larger prediction errors. Under geometric extrapolation, however, the model becomes overconfident: epistemic uncertainty increases but does not fully account for growing prediction errors. Finally, the framework is extended to three-dimensional wind-farm wakes, where the learned correction transfers to unseen layouts and posterior samples are propagated through the RANS solver, with the aleatoric component injected as a spatially correlated field, to obtain uncertainty bounds on the predicted wake flow.

infographic.key_insight: Bayesian Kolmogorov-Arnold networks provide inspectable Reynolds-stress closures with separate epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty estimates.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports uncertainty-aware RANS predictions, including wind-farm wake corrections that transfer to unseen layouts.
method: Learn univariate spline functions with variational posteriors over spline coefficients.
Enforce invariance, symmetry and tracelessness through a tensor basis; encourage realisability with soft regularisation.
Propagate posterior samples through RANS, injecting aleatoric uncertainty as a spatially correlated field.
infographic.evidence_signal: A controlled regression benchmark and turbulence applications show a favorable accuracy–calibration balance for spline-coefficient posteriors, calibrated in-distribution uncertainty, and transfer to unseen wind-farm layouts.
infographic.watch_item: Under geometric extrapolation, epistemic uncertainty increases but remains insufficient to capture growing prediction errors, leaving the model overconfident.
infographic.paper_title: Bayesian Kolmogorov-Arnold networks for trustworthy Reynolds-stress closures

title: Microdroplet Generator Surrogate Enhancement and Inverse Design Through an Uncertainty-Guided Framework
authors: David Gabriel Harispe, Matías Gerard, Pablo A. Kler
abstract: Microfluidic droplet generation is critical for many applications, yet efficient device design in high-dimensional parameter spaces remains computationally prohibitive due to complex multiphase flow dynamics. This work presents a unified methodology that couples adaptive surrogate enhancement with simulation-driven inverse design. High-fidelity Volume-of-Fluid simulations provide ground-truth data, while neural network ensembles predict flow regimes and droplet diameters. Ensemble-based uncertainty quantification identifies epistemic uncertainty using consensus levels for regime classification and the coefficient of variation for diameter prediction, revealing that uncertainty concentrates near regime transition boundaries where physics is highly sensitive to parameter perturbations. A physics-informed enrichment strategy targets these critical zones and addresses class imbalances by deploying additional targeted simulations and retraining the surrogates forming the ensembles. A framework that integrates Particle Swarm Optimization for constrained inverse design, balancing accuracy with predictive confidence and physical consistency is therefore proposed. Validation on independent test datasets demonstrates that the enriched ensembles achieve higher accuracy, with the fraction of predictions within the 0-3% error range on droplet diameter nearly doubling, and high-error cases (above 10%) dropping substantially. The inverse design procedure reliably identifies physically realizable configurations meeting target droplet sizes. This approach significantly reduces computational costs while ensuring reliable predictions, offering a framework with potential applicability to the optimization of a broad range of microfluidic systems.

infographic.key_insight: Uncertainty-guided simulation enrichment improves neural ensemble predictions for microdroplet generation and supports reliable inverse design.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework helps identify microfluidic configurations that meet target droplet sizes while reducing reliance on costly multiphase simulations.
method: Train neural network ensembles on high-fidelity Volume-of-Fluid simulations to predict flow regimes and droplet diameters.
Use regime consensus and diameter coefficient of variation to target additional simulations near uncertain transitions and address class imbalance.
Apply Particle Swarm Optimization for constrained inverse design, balancing accuracy, predictive confidence, and physical consistency.
infographic.evidence_signal: On independent test datasets, enrichment nearly doubled the fraction of diameter predictions with 0–3% error and substantially reduced cases above 10% error.
infographic.watch_item: Ensemble confidence may not guarantee accuracy outside the simulated design space; extrapolated designs warrant high-fidelity validation.
infographic.paper_title: Microdroplet Generator Surrogate Enhancement and Inverse Design Through an Uncertainty-Guided Framework

title: FlowReconBench: Accuracy, calibration and cost of learned and classical flow reconstruction from sparse sensors
authors: Nicolas Tricard, Linzheng Wang, Jason Chen, Sili Deng
abstract: Reconstructing full flow fields from sparse sensors requires prior assumptions about unmeasured regions and physical variables. Yet it remains unclear when learned models outperform classical estimators and which aspects of their predictions can be trusted. FlowReconBench evaluates ten learned and five classical methods on three regimes: a laminar cylinder wake across Reynolds numbers, two-dimensional Kolmogorov turbulence and a large-scale three-dimensional (3D) isotropic turbulence. Methods share leakage-controlled splits and sensor draws and are scored on per-channel error, ensemble spread, calibration, spectra and cost. The leading method changes for each regime. Classical methods perform strongly in low-order and dense-sensing regimes. On the cylinder wake, linear stochastic estimation and gappy proper orthogonal decomposition lead, including for unobserved pressure. In 3D, inverse-distance weighting matches the best learned methods on observed channels. Data-driven methods become superior at decreasing sensor density or poor sensor observability. On Kolmogorov flow, continuous ranked probability score and error yield different method rankings: generative models offer broader but underdispersed ensembles, while deterministic models prioritize pointwise error. Generative models balance this tradeoff through their sampler budget, with a larger budget improving ensemble quality at higher computational cost. In 3D, scaling tests demonstrate that queryable methods are flat in memory, while full-grid construction methods run out of memory. Observing only 2 of 4 fields leaves the problem kinematically underconstrained, yet a latent model can reproduce structural similarities to the ground truth.

infographic.key_insight: No reconstruction method wins across all flows: classical estimators remain competitive, while learned methods gain advantages with fewer sensors or poorly observed fields.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Sparse-sensor flow reconstruction should balance accuracy, uncertainty calibration and computational cost rather than defaulting to learned models.
method: Benchmark 10 learned and 5 classical methods across cylinder wakes, 2D Kolmogorov turbulence and large-scale 3D isotropic turbulence.
Use leakage-controlled splits and shared sensor draws for comparable evaluations.
Measure per-channel error, ensemble spread, calibration, spectra and computational cost.
infographic.evidence_signal: Classical methods lead on cylinder wakes, inverse-distance weighting matches top learned methods on observed 3D channels, and Kolmogorov rankings differ between pointwise error and probabilistic scoring.
infographic.watch_item: Generative ensembles remain underdispersed, and improving ensemble quality through larger sampling budgets increases computational cost.
infographic.paper_title: FlowReconBench: Accuracy, calibration and cost of learned and classical flow reconstruction from sparse sensors

title: Rigorously Certified Neural-Network Computation of Nonlinear Water Waves at Near-Machine Precision
authors: Michal Shavit, Yongji Wang, Tristan Buckmaster
abstract: We present a computational framework that combines machine-learning-based discovery with rigorous computer-assisted numerical certification and formal verification for strongly nonlinear partial differential equations. We demonstrate the approach for periodic gravity-capillary traveling water waves. Physics-informed neural networks are used as a search mechanism, with the wave profile, wave speed and, in continuation experiments, surface tension learned directly from the governing equations without training data. Through a staged training and refinement procedure, the neural networks achieve near-machine-precision residuals of the governing equations, even in strongly nonlinear regimes. A single formulation recovers high-amplitude Stokes waves, Crapper waves and Wilton ripples. Continuation from a high-amplitude Wilton ripple in surface tension reveals new high-amplitude candidate solutions. We freeze one candidate as an explicit finite representation and rigorously certify a uniform bound on its governing-equation residual using interval arithmetic, accounting for floating-point roundoff, Fourier truncation, aliasing and grid-to-continuum errors. This independently validates the neural-network accuracy. We formalize the certification argument in Lean, which machine-checks the deductions from certified numerical bounds to the residual theorem. Both the interval certification and formalization were developed with substantial assistance from a large language model, while the validity of the result remains independent of the language model: the numerical bounds are rigorously enclosed by interval arithmetic and the subsequent mathematical deductions are checked by the Lean kernel. Together, these steps provide a pipeline from neural discovery to rigorous numerical certification and machine-checked verification with auditable mathematical guarantees.

infographic.key_insight: Physics-informed neural networks discover strongly nonlinear water waves with near-machine-precision equation residuals, followed by rigorous residual certification and machine-checked verification for one candidate.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers an auditable route from AI-generated wave computations to certified equation-residual bounds for nonlinear free-surface flow modeling.
method: Learn periodic wave profiles, speeds and selected surface tensions directly from governing equations without training data.
Use staged training, refinement and continuation to recover known wave families and discover new candidates.
Certify one finite representation using interval arithmetic, then verify deductions from certified bounds in Lean.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports recovery of Stokes waves, Crapper waves and Wilton ripples, plus a certified uniform residual bound for one candidate accounting for roundoff, Fourier truncation, aliasing and grid-to-continuum errors.
infographic.watch_item: Certification covers one candidate’s equation residual; it does not by itself establish proximity to an exact solution or certify every discovered wave.
infographic.paper_title: Rigorously Certified Neural-Network Computation of Nonlinear Water Waves at Near-Machine Precision

title: A characteristic mapping method for dissipative evolution equations
authors: William Holman-Bissegger, Seth Taylor, Jean-Christophe Nave
abstract: The Characteristic Mapping (CM) method is a transport scheme which discretizes the Lagrangian flow map as a composition of spatial interpolants. This adaptive approximation technique has demonstrated novel resolution properties and the ability to efficiently simulate the fine scales of inviscid turbulent flows. In this work, we construct an extension of this approach to the solution of dissipative problems, including the Navier-Stokes equations. The extension lifts a general scalar evolution equation to a path in a group of diffeomorphisms, where the semigroup approach of the CM method can be exploited. We give an interpretation of this lift through the geometric framework of optimal transport. We then introduce a semidirect product evolution technique to perform the time stepping of the map components. The map is evolved based on the semi-Lagrangian CM approach, and its log-Jacobian is evolved explicitly by an exponential integrator. The numerical scheme is demonstrated to be high-order accurate and is tested on a range of canonical nonlinear dissipative equations. By retaining the resolution properties of the CM method, the approach shows a promising ability to simulate turbulent fluid flows across all Reynolds numbers.

infographic.key_insight: Extending characteristic mapping to dissipative equations preserves its fine-scale resolution strategy while enabling applications to Navier–Stokes flows.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could support efficient, high-resolution simulation of turbulent flows across a broad range of Reynolds numbers.
method: Lift scalar evolution equations to paths in a diffeomorphism group, interpreted through optimal transport.
Represent flow maps as compositions of spatial interpolants and evolve them with semi-Lagrangian characteristic mapping.
Use semidirect product time stepping with an exponential integrator for the map’s log-Jacobian.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports high-order accuracy and tests on canonical nonlinear dissipative equations, but provides no quantitative error or runtime results.
infographic.watch_item: Performance and robustness across all Reynolds numbers remain promising rather than established by the abstract’s reported evidence.
infographic.paper_title: A characteristic mapping method for dissipative evolution equations

title: Low-Rank Tensor Manifolds for Turbulent Field Reconstruction from Sparse Data
authors: Nazmus Sakib, Alexander G. Mychkovsky, Hessam Babaee
abstract: Reconstructing turbulent flow fields from sparse and irregular measurements remains challenging because the underlying inverse problem is severely underdetermined. Here we present MANTRA, a manifold-based tensor framework that represents each velocity component in a continuous tensor-product space while constraining its coefficient tensor to a low-rank Tucker manifold. This structure provides a compact, data-adaptive representation without requiring gridded observations or governing equations. Riemannian optimization and adaptive selection of rank and basis complexity enable the model to exploit coordinate-wise spatiotemporal correlations. In simulations of forced isotropic turbulence and flow over a cylinder, MANTRA recovers multiscale structures at sampling densities orders of magnitude below the underlying grids and remains accurate under Gaussian noise up to 20% of the peak velocity. It also recovers leading coordinate-wise correlation structures from sparse observations. Applied to experimental particle-tracking velocimetry of an oscillating impinging jet, MANTRA reveals time-evolving structures that are not apparent from the scattered measurements alone.

infographic.key_insight: MANTRA reconstructs multiscale turbulent velocity fields from sparse, irregular measurements using continuous tensor-product representations constrained to low-rank Tucker manifolds.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework can extract coherent flow structures from limited experimental measurements without requiring gridded observations or governing equations.
method: Represent each velocity component in a continuous tensor-product space.
Fit low-rank Tucker coefficient tensors using Riemannian optimization.
Adapt tensor rank and basis complexity to capture coordinate-wise spatiotemporal correlations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests on forced isotropic turbulence and cylinder flow report reconstruction at sampling densities orders of magnitude below the simulation grids and accuracy under Gaussian noise up to 20% of peak velocity, alongside an experimental oscillating-jet demonstration.
infographic.watch_item: Performance beyond the tested flows remains uncertain, particularly when sparse measurements do not sufficiently constrain the chosen low-rank representation.
infographic.paper_title: Low-Rank Tensor Manifolds for Turbulent Field Reconstruction from Sparse Data

title: A coupled lattice Boltzmann model for pore-scale mushy-layer dynamics with application to sea ice
authors: Nicola Trippella, Dario Maggiolo
abstract: A pore-scale lattice Boltzmann model is developed for reactive transport in phase-changing porous media, coupling solute transport in the liquid with conjugate heat transfer across the solid and liquid phases. Two methodological developments are introduced: a novel link-based Volume-of-Pixel formulation for direction-dependent interface motion, and a generalized Robin boundary treatment for solute redistribution at moving interfaces. The phase-change formulation is validated against thermal benchmarks, while the Robin treatment is assessed through literature test cases, exhibiting convergence rates between first and second order. The coupled model is then applied to a local pore-scale segment of a sea ice brine channel in a purely diffusive regime. The simulations recover the expected ideal mushy-layer behaviour under appropriate scale separation. At sea-ice-relevant concentration ratios, thermal perturbations produce relatively large variations in brine salinity, causing freezing rather than melting to reshape the pore geometry in a non-uniform way. The resulting framework provides a pore-scale numerical tool for resolving coupled temperature, solute redistribution, and phase-boundary dynamics in mushy layers.

infographic.key_insight: A coupled pore-scale lattice Boltzmann model shows how temperature-driven salinity changes can make freezing reshape sea-ice brine channels non-uniformly.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports pore-scale analysis of coupled heat transfer, solute redistribution, and evolving geometry in phase-changing porous media.
method: Couple liquid solute transport with conjugate heat transfer across solid and liquid phases.
Track direction-dependent interface motion using a link-based Volume-of-Pixel formulation.
Apply generalized Robin boundary conditions for solute redistribution at moving interfaces.
infographic.evidence_signal: Thermal benchmarks validate phase change, literature tests show first- to second-order convergence for the Robin treatment, and diffusive sea-ice simulations recover ideal mushy-layer behaviour under appropriate scale separation.
infographic.watch_item: The sea-ice application covers a local, purely diffusive pore segment; performance with advective transport or larger-scale channel networks remains unestablished here.
infographic.paper_title: A coupled lattice Boltzmann model for pore-scale mushy-layer dynamics with application to sea ice

title: Orientation and slip statistics of spheroids settling in turbulence
authors: Anubhab Roy
abstract: Small spheroids settling through turbulence are turned broadside-on by fluid inertia and tilted away by velocity gradients. We describe their orientation and slip statistics through the crossover from random orientation to alignment, in the overdamped limit. With quasi-static Stokes drag the leading inertial torque is an exact gradient flow on the orientation sphere, its potential quadratic in the cosine of the tilt and only rescaled by mobility anisotropy. The orientation performs an overdamped random walk in a quadratic well, and isotropic Gaussian white noise gives exactly a Boltzmann distribution. For forcing of finite correlation time, a closure keeps this form with its width set by linear response; it recovers the uniform density as settling vanishes and, for fixed-orientation forcing statistics, the aligned coefficient of rapid-settling theory, and errs most in the crossover. The root-mean-square lateral slip peaks where the alignment rate approaches the Kolmogorov rate, as faster settling strengthens the sideways drift at a given tilt but suppresses the tilt; the nearly shape-independent ratio, which tensor-forced simulations reproduce, lets a measured peak constrain the torque coefficient or dissipation rate for given forcing statistics. Dissipation intermittency enters as a lognormal superposition of Boltzmann distributions, which fattens the tails but leaves the leading aligned mean-square tilt unchanged. The superposition reproduces the shape of plate orientation distributions from direct numerical simulations, where a single Boltzmann distribution fails; published moments confirm the predicted spread beyond the weakest torques, and at strong alignment the measured fourth-order tilt moment lies between the two predictions.

infographic.key_insight: Settling spheroids transition from random orientation to broadside alignment, with lateral slip peaking when the alignment rate approaches the Kolmogorov rate.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For known forcing statistics, a measured lateral-slip peak could constrain the inertial torque coefficient or turbulent dissipation rate.
method: Model inertial reorientation as overdamped gradient flow in a quadratic orientation potential.
Use a Boltzmann orientation distribution, with linear-response closure for finite-correlation forcing.
Represent dissipation intermittency through a lognormal mixture of Boltzmann distributions.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tensor-forced simulations reproduce the nearly shape-independent slip-peak ratio, while the intermittent model captures plate-orientation distribution shapes from direct numerical simulations.
infographic.watch_item: The finite-correlation closure is least accurate in the random-to-aligned crossover, and the framework assumes overdamped dynamics with quasi-static Stokes drag.
infographic.paper_title: Orientation and slip statistics of spheroids settling in turbulence

title: Improving the accuracy of the momentum-exchange method in lattice Boltzmann methods
authors: Abbas Fakhari
abstract: In the lattice Boltzmann method (LBM), the momentum-exchange method (MEM) is widely used to evaluate hydrodynamic forces at fluid-solid interfaces due to its computational efficiency and geometric flexibility. However, when mapping complex geometries onto structured Cartesian grids, the physical boundary rarely intersects the lattice links exactly at their midpoints. This discrepancy violates an implicit assumption inherent to the conventional momentum-exchange (CME) formulation. In this study, we systematically analyze this geometric deficiency and demonstrate that it induces significant force inaccuracies, even in elementary flows where the solid boundary deviates from the midway position. To resolve this, we propose a modified momentum-exchange (MME) method that explicitly accounts for the exact boundary location along the lattice links, demonstrating enhanced accuracy for both flat and curved geometries. Furthermore, we address another critical issue with the interpolation-supplemented bounce-back (ISBB) schemes, and that is their inherent violation of local mass conservation. This mass leakage induces unphysical pressure buildup in the system, which compromises the accuracy and stability of the LBM. We propose a mass-conservative remedy for ISBB schemes that eliminates this leakage. Through a series of benchmark simulations of increasing complexity, we demonstrate that combining the proposed MME with the mass-corrected ISBB scheme drastically improves the fidelity of hydrodynamic force evaluations, establishing a robust framework essential for moving boundary problems and fluid-structure interactions.

infographic.key_insight: Accounting for the true fluid–solid boundary location and correcting mass leakage improves hydrodynamic force accuracy in lattice Boltzmann simulations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: More reliable force evaluation supports simulations of complex geometries, moving boundaries, and fluid–structure interactions.
method: Identify force errors caused by the conventional momentum-exchange method’s implicit midpoint-boundary assumption.
Modify momentum exchange to account for the exact boundary position along lattice links.
Apply a mass-conservative correction to interpolation-supplemented bounce-back schemes.
infographic.evidence_signal: Benchmark simulations of increasing complexity show improved force fidelity for flat and curved boundaries, though the abstract provides no quantitative error reductions.
infographic.watch_item: Implementation requires accurate boundary–link intersection locations and integration of the mass-conservation correction.
infographic.paper_title: Improving the accuracy of the momentum-exchange method in lattice Boltzmann methods

title: Eddies that ride the flow: a model of turbulence with Richardson dispersion and anomalous dissipation
authors: Raul Jimenez, Svitlana Mayboroda, Camillo de Lellis, David N. Spergel, Max Engelstein
abstract: We construct a divergence-free velocity field $\mathbf{u}(\mathbf{x},t)$ on $\mathbb{T}^{n}$ that is a genuine function of position and carries both defining properties of turbulent transport: Richardson pair dispersion and a dissipative anomaly. No synthetic field has carried both, because the frame that gives the first destroys the field the second requires. The key is a dichotomy: deforming a spectrally localised pattern smears it across scales, whereas pushing its generating centres forward and re-convolving leaves the spectral envelope exactly invariant --- so transporting the eddy centres preserves both cascade and frame. In the field the finite-size Lyapunov exponent obeys $ζ(R)=h(R)-1$ threshold by threshold within the scaling range, with a sweeping deficit $Δ_{\rm sw}=+0.038\pm0.019$, consistent with zero, against $+0.091\pm0.019$ for the frozen field on the same data, a gap that doubles at Navier--Stokes intermittency. Companion papers prove that this family shows Richardson dispersion and a dissipative anomaly (Fefferman and Mayboroda 2026), and that a scalar advected by this flow obeys Yaglom's relation (De Lellis 2026), at small Kubo number. Trajectories forget their starting point as the smallest eddy is removed: the median separation of pairs released from one point with independent Brownian kicks varies as $κ_{p}^{0.0333\pm0.0038}$ over 22 decades of particle diffusivity, against $κ_{p}^{1/2}$ for a smooth control. A scalar in the same field closes the exact scale-by-scale variance budget, four independently measured terms balancing the dissipation to 15\% over 1.2 decades with no adjustable constant, and reaches its inertial--convective asymptote $S_{L}=-χr$ to $0.9995\pm0.0018$ once the measured diffusive transfer is restored, while under an imposed mean gradient $χ$ changes by 14\% over a factor 5.8 in $κ$.

infographic.key_insight: Transporting eddy centres and re-convolving preserves the spectral envelope, enabling a divergence-free synthetic flow that combines Richardson pair dispersion with anomalous dissipation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The model offers a controlled testbed for studying turbulent particle transport and scalar mixing without resolving a full Navier–Stokes flow.
method: Advect eddy-generating centres rather than deforming the eddy patterns.
Re-convolve transported centres to preserve the spectral envelope.
Evaluate pair dispersion, trajectory separation and scale-by-scale scalar variance budgets.
infographic.evidence_signal: The sweeping deficit is 0.038 ± 0.019 versus 0.091 ± 0.019 for a frozen field, while independently measured scalar-budget terms balance dissipation within 15% over 1.2 decades.
infographic.watch_item: The cited companion proofs apply at small Kubo number; broader validity and engineering-flow performance remain to be established.
infographic.paper_title: Eddies that ride the flow: a model of turbulence with Richardson dispersion and anomalous dissipation

title: Interscale energy transfer in a propeller-driven homogeneous and isotropic turbulence generation device
authors: Luciano Hergenreder, Serge Simoëns, Cristián Escauriaza, Wernher Brevis
abstract: We investigate the interscale energy dynamics of nearly homogeneous isotropic turbulence (HIT) generated in a spherically forced, propeller-driven device. From a spatial perspective, by employing the Kármán-Howarth-Monin (KHM) framework, we analyze the scale-by-scale energy transfer without isotropy assumptions. In contrast to other forcing strategies, where regions with inverse and forward cascades often coexist in scale space, we show that spherical forcing produces a purely forward energy cascade across the entire scale space. While the energy distribution remains highly isotropic and orientation-averaged structure functions align with Kolmogorov's two-thirds law, the energy flux exhibits a directional dependence, suggesting a higher sensitivity to residual forcing asymmetries. Regarding the temporal dynamics, the reduced mean flow generated by this device allows us to investigate the temporal variability in conditions where Taylor's frozen turbulence hypothesis does not apply. Our results provide experimental validation of Tennekes' Eulerian frequency spectrum, where intermediate scales evidence an inertial-convective range with statistics determined by the integral velocity scale and the dissipation rate. Finally, we adopt a global approach to investigate whether the main turbulent scales can be linked to external experimental parameters. We propose a framework that captures the propeller frequency dependence of the main turbulent variables obtained in our measurements and those of previously reported HIT chambers. These findings contribute to the understanding of how external forcing influences the complex interscale energy dynamics of turbulent flows from a spatial, temporal, and global perspective.

infographic.key_insight: Spherical propeller forcing produces a purely forward energy cascade across scale space, even though energy flux retains directional dependence in nearly homogeneous isotropic turbulence.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The findings support the design and characterization of turbulence-generation chambers by linking forcing geometry and propeller frequency to turbulent energy dynamics.
method: Apply the Kármán–Howarth–Monin framework to scale-by-scale energy transfer without assuming isotropy.
Measure Eulerian temporal statistics under low mean flow, where Taylor’s frozen-turbulence hypothesis does not apply.
Develop a propeller-frequency scaling framework using current measurements and previously reported HIT chamber data.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments show orientation-averaged structure functions consistent with Kolmogorov’s two-thirds law and intermediate-scale frequency statistics supporting Tennekes’ Eulerian spectrum.
infographic.watch_item: Nearly isotropic energy distributions do not guarantee isotropic energy flux, which remains sensitive to residual forcing asymmetries.
infographic.paper_title: Interscale energy transfer in a propeller-driven homogeneous and isotropic turbulence generation device

title: Learned Surrogates of Three-Dimensional Magnetohydrodynamic Turbulence
authors: Semih Kacmaz, E. A. Huerta
abstract: Three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) turbulence, the flow of astrophysical and fusion plasmas, is costly to simulate. We present, to our knowledge, the first learned surrogates of three-dimensional resistive MHD turbulence, and compare three standard backbones in that role: a convolutional UNet, a shifted-window transformer and a Fourier neural operator. They are trained as autoregressive emulators of decaying MHD turbulence at a resolution of $128^3$ and Reynolds numbers of 1000, 3000 and 6000, on 500 simulations per Reynolds number, each with one two-stage procedure, single steps and then short rollouts, and stopped by one rule. Over a window of about one large-eddy turnover time, the UNet and the transformer reach relative velocity errors of 0.018 to 0.053 and keep the current sheets, the enstrophy, the current density and the energy spectra of the simulation; which of the two is the more accurate depends on the Reynolds number, the UNet leading at 3000 and 6000 and the transformer at 1000. Applied with the same backbones and training procedure to two public benchmarks, the models reach the lowest error reported to date on the isotropic turbulence set of FactFormer, 39% below the best published model. On the compressible MHD set of The Well, their rollout errors are a third to a half below those of the best of The Well's baselines. They also match a 1.3 B-parameter pretrained foundation model in its rollout windows, with 20-62 times fewer parameters. The code, the configuration of every model, the evaluation scripts and the data generator with the seed of every simulation will be released upon publication.

infographic.key_insight: Learned surrogates can emulate 3D resistive MHD turbulence over about one large-eddy turnover time, with UNet and transformer models achieving relative velocity errors of 0.018–0.053.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These models offer a potential route to reducing repeated simulation costs for astrophysical and fusion-plasma turbulence while retaining important flow and magnetic-field structures.
method: Compare a convolutional UNet, shifted-window transformer and Fourier neural operator.
Train autoregressively on 128³ decaying MHD simulations at Reynolds numbers 1000, 3000 and 6000.
Use single-step training followed by short-rollout training with a common stopping rule.
infographic.evidence_signal: Training uses 500 simulations per Reynolds number; public-benchmark evaluation reports 39% lower error than the best published FactFormer isotropic-turbulence result and one-third to one-half lower rollout errors than The Well's best baselines.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy is demonstrated over limited rollout windows; longer-term stability and generalization beyond the studied turbulence regimes remain unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Learned Surrogates of Three-Dimensional Magnetohydrodynamic Turbulence

title: The lattice Boltzmann machine
authors: Hua-Dong Yao, Sauro Succi
abstract: The lattice Boltzmann (LB) method is widely regarded as a very flexible and efficient solver for a broad class of transport phenomena in fluids, soft matter and related fields. In this paper, we posit that such flexibility is a direct result of its generative nature as a rule-driven information-processing machine. Its update, a relaxation toward a local target followed by a shift along the lattice, belongs to the same class of iterated relaxation dynamics as residual networks and transformers, with the difference that in LB the operators are fixed by conservation and symmetry rather than learned from data. We show that three properties of this update are sufficient to promote the emergence of closed macroscopic laws from the underlying iteration process, the physical content of the target deciding the specific law in question. A machine whose target is drawn at random generates the transport law predicted from its moments. A network given the same three properties on a graph, where there is no lattice, is trained on a traffic process and generates a conservation law of its own. The mechanism has a precise limit, where the damping of the non-conserved modes fails, and on the lattice the macroscopic law gives no warning of it. In this reading, LB is a lattice Boltzmann machine whose informing rules are supplied by physics rather than by training. Its three properties then state what a new ingredient should preserve when it enters an LB model, whether it comes from physics or from data.

infographic.key_insight: Lattice Boltzmann can be viewed as a physics-programmed information-processing machine whose relaxation-and-shift updates generate closed macroscopic transport laws.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This perspective offers a framework for assessing whether new physics-based or learned components preserve the structure needed for macroscopic transport behavior.
method: Frame lattice Boltzmann updates as iterated relaxation dynamics related to residual networks and transformers.
Identify three update properties sufficient for closed macroscopic laws to emerge.
Test the framework with random targets on a lattice and a traffic-trained network on a graph.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that random targets generate transport laws predicted by their moments and that a traffic-trained graph network generates its own conservation law, without providing quantitative metrics.
infographic.watch_item: The mechanism fails when non-conserved modes cease to be damped, and the lattice-level macroscopic law may not warn of this failure.
infographic.paper_title: The lattice Boltzmann machine

title: Novel hydrodynamic features in dissipative spin-polarized fluids
authors: Zbigniew Drogosz, Wojciech Florkowski, Jakub Witkowski
abstract: We investigate an extension of perfect spin hydrodynamics that includes dissipation in the spin sector. The presence of dissipation implies that antisymmetric parts of the energy-momentum tensor should be taken into account. Their form follows from the Navier-Stokes or Israel-Stewart theory, which introduces a priori unknown kinetic coefficients and relaxation times. We find that the inclusion of the antisymmetric parts of the energy-momentum tensor has twofold effects: i) they form source terms for the spin tensor allowing for the transfer between the spin and orbital parts of the total angular momentum (spin-orbit interaction) and ii) they appear in the conservation laws for the energy and linear momentum, indirectly affecting the spin dynamics. Numerical results are obtained for two boost-invariant expansion geometries: one-dimensional longitudinal motion (Bjorken model) and two-dimensional boost-invariant and cylindrically symmetric expansion. They indicate (for various choices of the spin kinetic coefficients and the relaxation times) that the spin polarization tensor approaches thermal vorticity. We also observe that Israel-Stewart dynamics on the way to local equilibrium approaches first the Navier-Stokes regime. In general, we find that the Israel-Stewart formalism naturally helps to consistently combine the conservation laws for linear and angular momentum, while the Navier-Stokes framework itself can lead to a disruption in the structure of the equations through the inclusion of terms involving derivatives of an order higher than one.

infographic.key_insight: Spin-sector dissipation couples spin and orbital angular momentum, with simulations indicating that spin polarization approaches thermal vorticity.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Consistent modeling of spin-polarized fluid dynamics requires accounting for antisymmetric stresses in both spin evolution and energy–momentum conservation.
method: Extend perfect spin hydrodynamics with dissipative antisymmetric energy–momentum terms.
Compare Navier–Stokes and Israel–Stewart formulations.
Simulate Bjorken flow and boost-invariant, cylindrically symmetric expansion.
infographic.evidence_signal: For various kinetic coefficients and relaxation times, simulations in both geometries indicate relaxation toward thermal vorticity, with Israel–Stewart dynamics first approaching the Navier–Stokes regime.
infographic.watch_item: Kinetic coefficients and relaxation times remain unspecified a priori, while the Navier–Stokes formulation can introduce higher-than-first-order derivatives that disrupt the equation structure.
infographic.paper_title: Novel hydrodynamic features in dissipative spin-polarized fluids

title: A physics-informed neural network method for pressure-driven turbine-blade optimization
authors: Yuan Huang, Francesca di Mare
abstract: We develop a physics-informed method for aerodynamic shape optimisation of turbine blades, treating the flow field and blade geometry as coupled unknowns. The method translates prescribed surface-pressure distributions into geometric modifications through pressure-target continuation and alternating flow-geometry updates. A differentiable representation of the blade surfaces allows their positions and orientations to be optimised within the current flow field, followed by flow re-adaptation to the modified boundaries. The inverse formulation uses the two-dimensional steady compressible Euler equations as physics constraints and is evaluated on the LS89 turbine cascade using 28 pressure-target points derived from experimental data. Starting from a modified profile and a warm-started flow network, the final pressure-side and suction-side root-mean-square fitting errors are 1.13% and 2.21% of inlet total pressure, respectively. Independent forward verification with SharC reproduces the principal surface-pressure trends of the experimental measurements, with remaining differences near the trailing edge. These results demonstrate the translation of experimental-origin loading data into geometric blade modifications through coordinated optimisation of the flow field and moving boundaries.

infographic.key_insight: A physics-informed neural network jointly updates turbine-blade geometry and flow to match prescribed surface-pressure targets.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method enables inverse aerodynamic design by translating desired blade loading into geometric modifications.
method: Constrain the flow with the 2D steady compressible Euler equations.
Optimise differentiable blade surfaces using pressure-target continuation.
Alternate geometry updates with flow re-adaptation.
infographic.evidence_signal: On the LS89 cascade with 28 experimental-derived pressure targets, final pressure- and suction-side RMS errors were 1.13% and 2.21% of inlet total pressure; independent SharC verification reproduced principal pressure trends.
infographic.watch_item: The 2D inviscid formulation does not resolve viscous or turbulent effects, and verification showed remaining trailing-edge pressure differences.
infographic.paper_title: A physics-informed neural network method for pressure-driven turbine-blade optimization
